morph.rootq: Steinhauer 1996a p.224: 'Stress always falls on the lexical stem, and usually on its penult. Some seemingly polysyllabic stems are stressed on the final syllable, apparently because they originally consisted of a monosyllabic stem and a petrified prefix (e.g. man'ap 'quick', bifel 'perempuan'). Stress may indicate a difference in the morphological build-up of otherwise identical words. For example: (3) qume [q'ume] 'house', qumen [q'umen] 'houses', versus qu-men [qum'en] 'I am ill' (stem -men).' Steinhauer 1996b p.479 (same dialect): 'Stress is fixed and generally falls on the penultimate syllable of the lexical stem that did not undergo apocope or metathesis. There are only a few…
morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined. The data are informant elicitation sessions: 'In this paper metathesis is discussed in the dialect of Miss Floribertha Lake ... I started working with her there in early January 1991 for about one week ... which enabled me to have regular sessions with her from March of that year' (1996a p.222); 'These data were collected on various occasions since 1992, both in Kupang and Jakarta, and always with my main informant' (1996b p.478). The illustrative material is mixed: ex.(1) p.223 marks stress in a whole sentence in phonetic notation…
morph.stmt: Mixed and light: verbs carry single-consonant subject prefixes (q-/m-/n-, 3PL additionally -n), nouns carry possessor suffixes (-k/-m/-n/-f) and phrase-final plural (-n/-in) and definite (-e/-i/-le) enclitics, nominalisation uses suffix -t/-s and circumfixes qa-...-t/-s, qa-...-b, q-...-q, while much grammatical work is done by subtractive/non-concatenative 'modification' — in Steinhauer's words (1996a p.231): 'Both languages [Dawanese and French] show phonological concatenation of grammatical words, while subtraction and modification with all major word classes are the morphological rule rather than the exception.'

qtr.text: 2.1.2. Stress is a force (dynamic) stress; it falls on the last syllable (in nominals); it causes reduction of the unstressed vowel (e.g. жогъул 'summer' — жогъла 'in summer'); in a polysyllabic verb there are two stresses — at the beginning and at the end, cf. аш-не-беса > аш-не-бса 'works'. Vowel length can also have a phonological character: эхне 'says' — э:хне 'talks endlessly, for a long time'; унекса 'eats' — у:некса 'eats endlessly, greedily'.

377.prule: Stress falls on the last syllable in nominals (жогъул 'summer', жогъла 'in summer'); a polysyllabic verb carries two stresses, one at the beginning and one at the end (аш-не-беса > аш-не-бса 'works'), which the source does not rank as primary and secondary.
377.srule: Polysyllabic verbs have two stresses, one at the beginning and one at the end (Dzheiranishvili 2001: 'в многосложном глаголе два ударения – в начале и в конце', аш-не-бса 'works'). Talibov & Maisak 2005 rank them: in polysyllabic words, especially verb forms, main stress final, secondary (weaker) stress initial ('главное ударение падает на последний слог, а побочное, менее сильное, – на начальный').

morph.rootq: Talibov & Maisak 2005: 181: «Ударение. Динамическое, порой интенсивное, падает на последний слог слова: адамáр ‛человек’ – адамарýх ‛люди’, хотя встречается и на первом слоге, особенно в словах, в состав которых входят указательные местоимения тте ‛тот’, ме ‛этот’, частица гьа и др. (ттéсагьат ‛тут же’, мéтаьр ‛так, так же, таким образом’ и т.п.). В многосложных словах, в особенности в глагольных формах, ударными бывают два слога: главное ударение падает на последний слог, а побочное, менее сильное, – на начальный. Впрочем, четких правил, регулирующих законы ударения, не выявлено.»…
morph.elicq: Talibov & Maisak 2005: 181 give only isolated citation forms (адамáр ~ адамарýх, ттéсагьат, мéтаьр) and close with «Впрочем, четких правил, регулирующих законы ударения, не выявлено»; no statement of how stress was elicited or measured (no frame, text or instrumental evidence mentioned).
morph.stmt: Udi is suffixing-agglutinative: «У.я. относится к языкам агглютинативного синтетического типа с элементами аналитизма» and «Словообразование. В основном суффиксальное» (Talibov & Maisak 2005: 181, 186); for the verb «Структура синтетической глагольной словоформы предельно проста:... она включает основу и суффиксальный словоизменительный показатель» and «особых словоизменительных префиксов или инфиксов в удинском языке нет, хотя префиксальная либо инфиксальная позиции могут быть заняты некоторыми видами клитик» (Maisak 2008: 98, 105) — the only pre-root material being the negative/prohibitive clitics (te=, ma=, nu-) and fossilised spatial preverbs, with person clitics enclitic or endoclitic.

tn.quote: СЛОГ И ПРОСОДИЯ 1. Типичные структуры слога: CV и CVC. В единичных словах зафиксированы конечные комплексы. 2. Фарингализация распространяется по всему слову при отсутствии увулярных и шипящих. ... 3. Акцентная система не изучена. Словесное ударение отсутствует, размещение фразового акцента в слове не исследовалось. Возможно наличие слогового тона.
tn.translation: SYLLABLE AND PROSODY 1. Typical syllable structures: CV and CVC. In isolated words final clusters are recorded. 2. Pharyngealization spreads over the whole word in the absence of uvulars and shibilants. ... 3. The accentual system has not been studied. Word stress is absent; the placement of the phrasal accent within the word has not been investigated. The presence of syllabic tone is possible.
tn.cite: Kibrik, A. E. & S. V. Kodzasov. 1990. Sopostavitel'noe izuchenie dagestanskix jazykov. Imja. Fonetika. Moskva: Izd. MGU. Sec. 22 'Udinskij jazyk (s. Nidzh)', Fonetika p.347.
tn.locator: p.347, sec. 22 'Удинский язык (с. Нидж)', 'Слог и просодия' items 1-3 (last lines of the page)
tn.note: Tone unresolved: Kibrik & Kodzasov 1990 (Nidzh) say the accent system is unstudied, word stress absent, 'syllabic tone possible'. Dzheiranishvili 2001 does not discuss tone (final dynamic stress).

378.dq: The stress is quantity-sensitive and falls on the most right bimoraic vowel or, in the absence of bimoraic vowels, on the most right vowel in the word. In affixes, word-final high vowels are extrametrical with respect to stress.
378.dloc: Nikolaeva & Tolskaya 2001, Ch. 1 Introduction, 'Phonology' overview, p. 33
378.heavy: Long and laryngealized vowels are bimoraic and attract the stress; short vowels are monomoraic and coda consonants do not provide a mora (closed syllables are light).
378.dflt: final syllable (rightmost vowel) when the word has no bimoraic vowel
378.prule: Primary stress on the rightmost long or laryngealized (bimoraic) vowel; if the word has none, on the final vowel; word-final short high vowels of inflectional affixes are skipped (extrametrical) (Nikolaeva & Tolskaya 2001:33, 60). The older Russian descriptions (Sunik 1968:213, Kormushin 1998:84) instead give a quantity-insensitive frame: dynamic accent on the first syllable and a pitch rise on the last.
378.srule: Initial-syllable prominence per the Russian descriptions behind the st2 coding: Kormushin 1998:84 - force accent on the first (root) syllable (for him the stress proper), musical pitch rise on the last; Sunik 1968:213 - 'weak expiratory stress on the first syllable, tonic (musical) on the last'. Gordon 2002:500 codes the initial one as the secondary stress and, citing Nikolaeva & Tolskaya 2001, as suppressed or very weak in disyllables (fn. 31: uncertain). Tolskaya 2011:27 (Bikin dialect, restating N&T 2001:33-95) instead: 'Secondary stress is less intense and in polysyllabic words can fall on the last syllable' (when the main stress is on a non-final bimoraic vowel); first-vowel prominence there is emphatic stress with rising pitch. N&T 2001 3.6.3 (pp. 90-94) not yet read.
378.quote: As distinct from regular short vowels, long and laryngealized vowels are associated with two moras and typically bear word stress. ... The stress is quantity-sensitive and falls on the most right bimoraic vowel or, in the absence of bimoraic vowels, on the most right vowel in the word. In affixes, word-final high vowels are extrametrical with respect to stress.
378.idn: Southern dialect of Udihe (Bikin and Iman rivers); data from Krasnyi Yar on the river Bikin; a few examples from the Northern dialect (Khor, Anyui, Samarga) (a named variety of the language); data: fieldwork conducted between 1989 and 1997 in the settlement of Krasnyi Yar on the river Bikin (N&T 2001: vii); Tolskaya…
378.exq_: In affixes, word-final high vowels are extrametrical with respect to stress. (p. 33) ... the word-final syllable with a short high vowel (in inflectional affixes) is extrametrical with respect to stress placement rules ... for example, wa:-mi 'kill (INF)'. (p. 60)

378.sec_quote: Удыхейское слово обладает двояким ударением. На первом (корневом) слоге делается силовой акцент, это собственно ударение. Последний слог слова получает музыкальное повышение тона. Серединные слоги не претерпевают редукции, поэтому динамическое ударение первого слога не столь выделяется, как ударный слог в словах русского языка.

secx.sec_quote_tr: The Udihe word has a double stress. On the first (root) syllable a force accent is made; this is the stress proper. The last syllable of the word receives a musical rise in pitch. Medial syllables do not undergo reduction, so the dynamic stress of the first syllable does not stand out as much as the stressed syllable in Russian words.

tn.quote: only in the most innovative varieties of Bikin and Iman, it became the main (and in Iman Udihe the only) distinctive feature [+tone]. Thus, these varieties should be classified as tonal … The term stress or accent is not appropriate here. … Contrastive prosodic patterns depend on the presence of a laryngealized vowel and on its place in the word. Contrastive prosodic patterns are, in fact, linguistic tones. Thus, Udihe and especially its southern varieties became a tonal language of the type of languages with low tone density, like Scandinavian dialects or Latvian.

378.cfw: Every source puts the main stress on the last syllable by default, but Nikolaeva and Tolskaya 2001 (restated in Tolskaya 2011 and adopted by Schiering and van der Hulst 2010) move it to the rightmost long or laryngealized vowel when the word has one, while the older Russian descriptions in Sunik 1968 and Kormushin 1998, which Gordon 2002 and StressTyp2 follow, give a weight-insensitive final stress with a weak initial stress.

qtr.text: 2.1.2. Word stress in Udmurt is dynamic and falls -- except in late Russian borrowings, which keep the stress of the original, and in certain verbal, pronominal and adverbial forms -- on the last syllable of the word. ... [Imperative] The plural is formed with the suffix -e(-le) (conj. I) or -le (conj. II): myn-e(le) 'go!', vera-le 'say!'. In all cases the stress is moved to the first syllable of a polysyllabic verb.

379.srule: Not described within the word in Kel'makov 1993 (§2.1.0-2.2.3, pp.241-243 read; §2.1.2 gives only final primary stress). The chapter's one mention of secondary (побочное) stress is phrase-level: function words are 'чаще безударно или имеет на себе побочное ударение' (more often unstressed or carry a secondary stress) relative to content words.

380.dq: In Uigur, as in other Turkic languages, the accent falls usually on the terminal syllable of the word ... Significative words in Uigur (which include substantives, adjectives, numerals, pronouns, verbs and adverbs) ... have an independent accent ... Subordinate words do not have any independent meaning and express only srammatical relations between words; they do not carry an independent accent

morph.rootq: Engesæth, Yakup & Dwyer 2009, Introduction §3 'Word Accent (Stress) Patterns', pp.3-4: 'In Uyghur, stress is mostly determined by the length of syllables. This means that a syllable which is closed (i.e., ends in consonants [CVC or CVCC]) tends to attract stress, while a syllable which is open (i.e. ends in a vowel [CV]) does not. If this seems confusing, until you learn the principles below, a general rule of thumb could be: stress the last syllable of the stem, e.g. ayagh "foot," Turpan'gha "to Turfan." ... While stress is most likely to fall on the last syllable, certain sounds and suffixes attract or repel stress ... Stress-attracting suffixes: e.g. -GAn, -Gu, -(A)m, -(I)wat ...…
morph.elicq: Introduction §3 p.3: 'Uyghur accent (stress or high pitch, which we will for convenience call stress) is not well understood, yet some general remarks can be made to aid language learning. ... (In the vocabulary lists, we underline stressed syllables.)' — no statement of how stress placements were determined; the marked forms are citation forms in vocabulary lists (the textbook is accompanied by audio of constructed dialogues, Preface p.vii, but the stress remarks are not tied to it).
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: 'Uyghur is an agglutinative language, meaning that potentially many suffixes (denoting person, number, case, mood, etc.) are usually all attached to one word stem. For example "to your house," the main word, house, occurs first, and the modifying element are attached directly to the right and written all in one word: öyingizge (öy-ingiz-ge, lit. "home-your-to")' (Engesæth, Yakup & Dwyer 2009, Introduction §1.2, p.1); noun template N+lAr+Poss+Case (Lesson 11 §3.5), verb e.g. oqu-wat-qan-im-da read-CONTINUOUS-INDEFINITE.PAST-my-at.

tn.quote: it is demonstrated on the basis of acoustic measurements that Uyghur is a stress language that only uses edge-marking intonation … This suggests that although Uyghur can be described as a stress language, stress and intonational tone are independent. … There were no significant effects of stress on f0. … These results support treating Uyghur as a stress language with only edge-marking intonation. … Because of the absence of head-marking tones in Uyghur … f0 does not associate with prominent syllables, but rather with the edges of phrases.

tn.note: Not a tone language: no lexical tone and no pitch accents; f0 marks only phrase edges (post-lexical AP, ip and IP boundary tones). Word stress, cued by duration alone, is independent of pitch.

381.dq: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root. With the addition of suffixes stress shifts to the resulting penultimate syllable. However, with the addition of enclitics stress does not shift to the right. Each vowel counts as the nucleus of a separate syllable. Although each vowel is a syllable nucleus and stress falls on the penultimate vowel, there is a blurring that occurs under c…

381.srule: None within the word base (one penultimate stress per base). Minor stresses only at the phrase/clitic-group level: non-nuclear word bases (incl. disyllabic prefix clusters like mòme-, pòka- and runs of two or more monosyllabic particles like tò-hi-) keep a reduced penultimate stress, and the phrase-final syllable takes a minor stress when the phrase ends in a two-syllable enclitic or in two or more particles (/mòme-pòka-áhi'/ 'to love each other', /ra-tudúi'-mi-ta-kà/ 'it was taught to us'). Not mentioned in Martens 1995 sec. 2.3 (the StressTyp2 source).
381.quote: 3.1.1 A word base is defined as a phonological/lexical unit of two or more syllables, either simple or derived. Word bases include both content words (nouns, verbs and adverbs) and grammatical function words (prefix clusters, multisyllabic enclitics). In a word base, stress is always penultimate. [...] 3.1.4 [...] Derivational suffixes, such as the /-a/ noun-forming suffix in (18b), form a new grammatical stem. 381.sec_quote: (a) The word base that forms the nucleus of the phrase receives primary stress. This is of course the main content word. The stresses of all other word bases preceding it are reduced slightly. The stresses of all word bases following it are reduced greatly. (b) If the phrase ends in a two-syllable enclitic or in two or more particles, the final syllable receives a minor stress.

In words of four syllables or more, a secondary stress attaches to the preceding syllable but one. ... It should be noted that stress placement applies after all morphophonemic processes have applied. morph.elicq: The stress section (§4.3) gives no statement of how stress was observed; it lists isolated citation forms (['ni] 'tree', ['nesi] 'pawpaw', [ni'mova] 'outrigger pole', [ˌsesi'maŋsi] 'index finger') and two inflected/derived pairs. morph.stmt: Predominantly prefixing: 'In its derivational morphology, Ura is fairly typical of Oceanic languages in that it makes productive use of prefixes and compounding, and less productive use of suffixes' and 'there is prefixal marking of pronominal subject categories on verbs in Ura, and there is a particularly rich inflectional set of tense-aspect-mood markers... discontinuously marked by combinations of morphotactically separate prefixes', while object suffixation is 'significantly less well developed... than we find in Sye' (§1.5 pp.8-9); the verb template is SUBJECT-(PRIOR PAST)-(ITERATIVE)-(NEGATIVE)-(EM-)-STEM (p.157), with suffixes limited to object pronouns on a few verbs, post-object…

382.sec_rule: In words of four or more syllables one secondary stress falls two syllables to the left of the primary, i.e. on the pre-antepenultimate syllable (["sesi'maŋsi] 'index finger' = 1010); two- and three-syllable words carry the primary only. Crowley states a single secondary stress and marks no word longer than four syllables, so iteration in words of six or more syllables is not stated in the source (the iterative 'even-numbered from the right' reading is Gordon 2002 / StressTyp2's coding).

Polysyllabic words in context cannot obscure their inherent stress. Monosyllabic words have their stress reduced considerably when the primary stress of a stress group is assigned somewhere else. Stress also plays a role in the morphology.' Pick 2020:31: 'Reesink (1987: 39-40) characterizes stress in Usan as phonemic, and illustrates this with minimal pairs that differ only in stress, such as [go.ˈbi] 'a tree', and [ˈgo.bi] 'taro seedling''…
morph.elicq: No explicit methods statement is available in the accessible excerpt. The description itself rests on (i) lexical minimal pairs cited as words — '[go.ˈbi] 'a tree', and [ˈgo.bi] 'taro seedling'' (Pick 2020:31 < Reesink 1987:39-40; StressTyp2 words ˈgugum/guˈgum, ˈgobi/goˈbi) — and (ii) observations of words in running context/stress groups: 'Polysyllabic words in context cannot obscure their inherent stress. Monosyllabic words have their stress reduced considerably when the primary stress of a stress group is assigned somewhere else.' (Reesink 1987:39 via StressTyp2). Coded 'mixed' on that basis; strictly, the elicitation procedure is unstated in what could be read.
morph.stmt: Usan is overwhelmingly suffixing and verb-centred: subject person-number/tense portmanteaux, future -ib-/-ub-, imperative, uncertain future, switch-reference (SS/DS), nominaliser -au, causative -si, benefactive ('give') and verbaliser -r all follow the root, while the only prefixes are the object/recipient person prefixes on (a subset of) transitive verbs and reciprocal qi- in that same slot; nouns are nearly bare (kin plural -eb, enclitic postposition -t; possessor, definiteness, negation and interrogation are free words). Pick 2020:31-32, summarising Reesink 1987: 'Northern Adelbert languages also follow the usual ordering of agreement affixes on the verb, with objects marked by prefixes…

385.prule: Primary (dynamic) stress falls on the final syllable of the word as a rule and stays final as stressed suffixes are added (Kononov 1960:52-53 §51; Sjoberg 1963:24 /ortɔ́q/ > /ortɔqlár/ > /ortɔqlarí/ > /ortɔqlarigá/; Raun 1969 'In most disyllabic words the marking stress is on the last syllable... Also in longer words the marking stress is on the last syllable'); quantity-insensitive. Enumerated classes take non-final stress: imperatives, 1st-person optatives, cardinal numerals, many adverbs/pronouns/interrogatives/interjections (initial), unstressed suffixes and enclitic particles (stress on the preceding syllable), recent Russian loans (source stress), disyllabic Arabic/Persian conjunctions and adverbs, some names, har-/hech- compounds and reduplications.
385.srule: Only weaker 'musical' (pitch) prominences are reported, with hedges: Kononov 1960:52-53 §51 puts a secondary pitch rise on the first syllable of trisyllables; in 4-5-syllable words the secondary stands one unstressed syllable apart from the final main stress (i.e. on the antepenult) and in 6+-syllable words two syllables apart, with a tertiary prominence on the first syllable (rhythm diagrams p. 53); his fn. 1 (p. 53) records the view that these pitch rises are not stresses at all. Raun 1969: 'a secondary stress... may appear on the first syllable, and in longer words a tertiary stress may occur'. Not coded on the rule string.
385.quote: Все слова узбекского языка в отношении акцентуации могут быть разбиты на две группы: 1) слова с силовым ударением на последнем слоге; 2) слова с силовым ударением не на последнем слоге. § 51. Силовое ударение на последнем слоге наблюдается, как правило, в двусложных именах существительных, прилагательных, глаголах … [p. 53] В многосложных словах силовое ударение, как правило, падает на последний слог … [p. 54] § 53. Силовое ударение не на последнем слоге имеет место в следующих случаях: 1. Во всех лицах повелительного наклонения, в 1-м л. ед. и мн. ч. желательного наклонения и в именах числит…
385.loc: pp. 52-55, §§50-53 'Slovesnoe udarenie' (word stress; phrasal stress is §57, p. 56)

Фактический материал, иллюстрирующий положения Грамматики, извлечен из современной художественной прозы, отчасти из поэзии, прессы и публицистики.' The stress chapter (§§50-56) cites prior descriptions (А. Ғуломов 'Ўзбек тилида урғу', Поливанов 1933, Kissen) and gives isolated word forms with accent marks; no elicitation procedure, frame or instrumental basis is stated.
morph.stmt: Kononov 1960 §63 p.63: 'Узбекское слово может состоять из чистой основы, а также из основы и аффикса (или аффиксов), который присоединяется к основе справа и обслуживает лексические (словообразовательные) или грамматические (формообразовательные) задания' — i.e. exclusively suffixing/agglutinative (e.g. сув-сиз-лиг-имиз-дан 'because of our waterlessness'); the only prefixes are a handful of borrowed Tajik-Persian adjectival prefixes бе-, ба-, но- on loan stems (§178) and preposed partial reduplication in intensive adjectives (қип-қизил, §55).

tn.quote: Ўзбек тилида ҳам мусиқий урғу йўқ, аммо унда чўзиқлик белгиси ва зарб бор. Бу белгилар урғули бўғинни шу сўздаги урғусиз бўғинлардан ажратиш имконини беради. ... Демак, ўзбек тилидаги сўз урғусида зарб биринчи ўринда туради, шунга кўра уни динамик урғу деб баҳолаш мақсадга мувофиқдир. Мусиқий (тоник, мелодик) урғу япон, хитой, корейс тилларига хосдир.
tn.translation: Uzbek too has no musical stress, but it does have the length feature and force (intensity). These features make it possible to distinguish the stressed syllable from the unstressed syllables of the word. ... Thus in Uzbek word stress force comes first, so it is appropriate to assess it as dynamic stress. Musical (tonic, melodic) stress is characteristic of Japanese, Chinese and Korean.
tn.cite: Jamolxonov, Hasanboy. 2009. O'zbek tilining nazariy fonetikasi ('O'zbek tili'dan o'quv qo'llanma). Toshkent: Fan.
tn.locator: p.165, 32-§ Урғу (Акцентема), I.1 (фонетик табиатига кўра сўз урғуси)
tn.note: States Uzbek has no musical (tonic/melodic) accent: word stress is dynamic and final; pitch appears only in syntagma/phrase intonation.

385.cfw: Sjoberg 1963 calls Uzbek stress phonemic but places it on the final syllable by default, and Athanasopoulou, Vogel & Dolatian 2020 read the same facts as Turkish-type final stress with pre-stressing suffixes and lexical exceptions and find acoustic support for final prominence, so excluding Uzbek as a lexical-stress language is the weaker reading.

386.dq: All the Balto-Finnic languages appear to have fixed initial primary accent. ... The (nearly) extinct language Votic (Ariste 1968) appears to have secondary accents on odd-numbered syllables. Also, final syllables can take secondary accent irrespective of whether they are heavy or light, except for case suffixes, which are never accented.
386.dloc: van der Hulst, Hendriks & van de Weijer 1999, sec. 7.2.2.4 'Uralic languages', paragraph 'Estonian, Finnish, Karelian, Votic, Livonian (Balto-Finnic)', pp. 449-450
386.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable (van der Hulst et al. 1999:449 'fixed initial primary accent'; Ariste 1948 §16 'normaalselt esimesel silbil', with a few obscured compounds and recent Russian loans stressed non-initially).
386.srule: Secondary stress on the third (and fifth) syllable, i.e. on odd-numbered non-initial syllables, a word-final odd syllable included irrespective of its weight; case suffixes never carry secondary stress (Ariste 1948 §16; van der Hulst et al. 1999:450).
386.quote: All the Balto-Finnic languages appear to have fixed initial primary accent. When it comes to secondary accent, however, there are a number of differences. ... The (nearly) extinct language Votic (Ariste 1968) appears to have secondary accents on odd-numbered syllables. Also, final syllables can take secondary accent irrespective of whether they are heavy or light, except for case suffixes, which are never accented.
386.loc: sec. 7.2.2.4 'Uralic languages', paragraph 'Estonian, Finnish, Karelian, Votic, Livonian (Balto-Finnic)', p. 449 (first two sentences) and p. 450 (Votic sentences)
386.idn: Votic (vdH 1999); lääne-vadja, Kattila murrak (Ariste 1948); западный диалект: кракольский (J, Jõgõperä) и лужицкий (L, Luuditsa) говоры (Agranat 2007); data: vdH 1999: no place/date, reports Ariste 1968. morph.stmt: Votic is exclusively suffixing (plus stem-internal alternation): in Ariste (1948) every inflectional category — the sixteen cases (§19–35), plural -D/-i- (§20, §41), the receding possessive suffixes (§67), subject person, past -i-, conditional -isi-, imperative, potential and impersonal markers (§76–95) — and every derivational 'tuletusliide' (§143–145) follows the stem ('Pöördsõna tüvele liituvad vaid pöördetunnused', §80: 'only the person endings are attached to the verb stem'), supplemented by consonant gradation and final-vowel lengthening (genitive/partitive/illative, §21–24); the only preposed grammatical word is the free, inflected negative auxiliary en/eD/eB (§103), and no prefix…

386.sec_rule: Secondary stress on the odd-numbered syllables after the initial primary (3rd, 5th...), including a word-final odd syllable regardless of its weight; case suffixes never carry secondary stress.
386.sec_quote: The (nearly) extinct language Votic (Ariste 1968) appears to have secondary accents on odd-numbered syllables. Also, final syllables can take secondary accent irrespective of whether they are heavy or light, except for case suffixes, which are never accented.

corr.head: StressTyp2 codes a fixed pattern that its source does not state
corr.detail: StressTyp2 codes penultimate primary stress with secondary pattern alternating from the last syllable; the description it cites (Fox 1979, pp. 7-8) calls stress phonemic, with minimal pairs, and says only that primary stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable in the majority of cases. The language is therefore not listed under fixed stress.

387.dq: An examination of words of all lengths (up to seven syllables) shows that in the majority of cases, primary stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable. Primary stress may not go back past the fifth syllable from the end of the word.
387.prule: Stress is phonemic (minimal pairs differing only in stress position). In the majority of words primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable and it never lies further back than the fifth syllable from the end; verbs, nouns and adjectives tend to keep the stress of their simplest form when affixed.
387.quote: In Big Nambas, stress is phonemic, as shown by the following contrasting examples: [i.'pa.li] 'he will burn it' [i.pa.'li] 'he will tie (it) to..' [a.'ɣau] 'wife of the chief' ['a.ɣau] 'go away!' Stress is partly predictable, and the following principles may be discerned. ... An examination of words of all lengths (up to seven syllables) shows that in the majority of cases, primary stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable. Primary stress may not go back past the fifth syllable from the end of the word.
387.loc: pp. 7-8, sec. 1.2.1 Stress, 1.2.1.1 Principle One, 1.2.1.2 Principle Two
387.idn: Big Nambas language ['θ̥ənɛn tautʰ], North Malekula (author at Brenwei, N.W. morph.rootq: §1.2.1.1 Principle One (p.8): 'An examination of words of all lengths (up to seven syllables) shows that in the majority of cases, primary stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable. Primary stress may not go back past the fifth syllable from the end of the word.' §1.2.1.2 Principle Two (p.8): 'Words which may take affixation (i.e. verbs, nouns and adjectives) tend to keep the stress on the syllable which is stressed in the words' simplest forms.'…
morph.elicq: 'An examination of words of all lengths (up to seven syllables) shows that in the majority of cases, primary stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable.' (§1.2.1.1, p.8). No elicitation method is stated; the evidence presented is transcribed single words and short affixed forms, plus phrase-level shifts in §1.2.1.3 ('Certain monosyllables following words stressed on the penultimate cause the stress to move forward to the ultima', e.g. /pe.ˈta.lu/ 'I will go to the garden': /pe.ta.ˈlu lel/ '...straight away'). Fieldwork basis: c. ten years' residence at Brenwei (Preface, Acknowledgements p.viii).
morph.stmt: Fox (§2.5.0, p.48): 'A verb may be described as an inflected stem, which expresses mode, actor, aspect, number and manner of action'; his affix chart (§2.5.2, pp.51-53) has six orders of prefixes before the stem (co-ordinator/actor-mode, necessity, aspect, negative, number, habituative) and three orders of suffixes after it (stem modifiers/manner, ability, pronoun object/benefactive), while nouns take possessive suffixes and the derivational/article prefixes na-, ni-, ter- and the quantifier prefix ar- 'all' -- i.e. obligatory inflection (subject-mood, aspect, negation, number) is prefixal and object, possessor, manner/applicative and ability marking is suffixal. Census after adjudication…

387.sec_rule: Fox speaks of 'primary stress' and transcribes two stress degrees (marks ' and ") in five-syllable words and in one affixed form (/"ƀə.tə.mi.'en.an/ 'his love'), i.e. a second stress mark two syllables after the first in the pentasyllables (syllables 2 and 4) and three after it in 'his love' (syllables 1 and 4); no rule for the secondary stress is stated and the text never uses the word 'secondary' (a full-text search: only 'secondary necessity particle', §2.5.3.2, p. 61). Which mark is primary is not explained: the heading 'Primary Stress on the Penultimate' fits " = primary in the pentasyllables, while shorter words carry ' alone.
387.sec_quote: Examples of Primary Stress on the Penultimate Syllable: Pentasyllables: /i.'pu.tak."ma.ni/ 'he will spoil it' ... Quadrisyllables: /in.ⁿdu.'la.ni/ 'he moved it' /pa.ti.'r̃a.ni/ 'put it up'
387.sec_loc: §1.2.1.1 Principle One, p. 8; also §1.2.1.2 p. 8 ('his love')

corr.head: StressTyp2's coding matches the source only in part
corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Waiwai: In words of all sizes, primary stress falls on the final syllable." The source gives: Two-syllable words: normally final (shifts when certain particles follow). Nouns/adverbs with CV pattern: three syllables normally final, four syllables penult; 'in either case stress falls on the syllable following the syllable having the long vowel' (long vowels only in sigma1/sigma2). Verbs and deverbal words: usually penult or final, 'more study is needed to define the rules'. Antepenult only in uninvolved-past collective verb forms. — StressTyp2 (entry, after Gordon 2002 / Hawkins 1952) codes fixed final stress at all lengths with no secondary.

contra.head: The rule as stated does not fit the source's own examples
contra.detail: Only 13 of 19 words that the source marks for stress come out as the stated rule predicts. Rule as we formalized it: Input: the word's syllables coded L/H, H = the syllable containing the word's (single) long vowel. Source facts used to code H (Hawkins 1998:152-154): at most one long vowel per word.

'[In] nouns or adverbs having three syllables and having a CV pattern stress normally occurs on the last syllable. If they have four syllables, the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. In either case stress falls on the syllable following the syllable having the long vowel.' ... 'In finite verbs and in words derived from verb stems the stress occurs usually on the penultimate or final syllable.' p.156: 'The only examples we have of stress in this position [antepenultimate] occur with verbs in the uninvolved past tense collective number.…
morph.elicq: Hawkins 1998 gives no statement of how stress was determined; the section rests on the author's decades of field observation and is hedged throughout: p.155 'But if such words are followed by certain particles (I am not sure if the rule holds for all particles or not), not only does length develop on the last syllable of the first word, but the stress moves from the first word to the particle'; p.156 'More study is needed to define the rules of such stress.' morph.stmt: Hawkins gives no one-line typological summary; his statements amount to: person is prefixal and everything else suffixal -- 'The person-marking prefixes show a split between subject and object person markers, which constitute two distinct sets. 389.srule: One secondary stress per word near the right edge: on the antepenult in words of five or more syllables (optionally on the penult instead), on the penult in four-syllable words (avoiding clash with the initial primary), none in words of three or fewer syllables (Gordon 2002 after Hudson 1978). morph.rootq: "Walmatjari does not have this contrast of stress. All words are stressed on the first syllable. In long words other syllables are also stressed. This does not mean that stress is unimportant. A Walmatjari word with incorrect stress can be unintelligible to the listener. The name 'Jukuna is virtually unrecognisable when the stress is altered from the first to the second syllable and it becomes Ju'kuna." (Hudson & Richards, WP SIL-AAB B-1, Part 2 §5.2, p.73). The statement is framed on the WORD, not the root; but since "The root of a Walmatjari word is always first" (§7, p.83) the word-initial syllable is always root-initial. Related: "The verbal auxiliary never takes clause stress"…
morph.elicq: Word stress is presented only through isolated citation words and a personal name: "In pronouncing the following Walmatjari words remember to stress the first part. yara 'well', mana 'tree', luwa 'Hit it with a missile!', wamulu 'eagle', lanani 'was spearing'" (Part 2 §5.2 p.73), with "A cassette recording of the words in Sections 3 and 5 accompanies this workpaper" (Introduction p.v). No frame sentences or measurements are mentioned. (By contrast Hudson 1981's clause-/sentence-level stress and intonation description rests on texts: "Most data presented here is from text material recorded on tape", WP A-5 p.245.)
morph.stmt: "Walmatjari is a suffixing language and many words in English have suffix equivalents in Walmatjari... The root of a Walmatjari word is always first and there may be many suffixes" (Hudson & Richards, WP B-1 Part 2 §7, p.83; illustrated with karla-ngu-jangka-warnti-wu-mipa 'the ones from the west only'); person/number of subject and object are likewise suffixes, on the second-position auxiliary root ("As many as five morphemes can be suffixed to the auxiliary root", Hudson 1976 n.3) — no prefixes or proclitics are described anywhere.

ev.text: Primary stress occurs normally on the first syllable of a word, with secondary stress on third and fifth syllables - except that final syllables are unstressed in connected speech. ... The final stress and aspiration appear to be suprasegmental features marking the end of an utterance, as well as emphasis.

morph.rootq: §2.1 Stress, p.5: 'Primary stress occurs normally on the first syllable of a word, with secondary stress on third and fifth syllables - except that final syllables are unstressed in connected speech. The first syllable of a two-syllable suffix receives secondary stress. Where the suffix attaches to a two-syllable stem, the final syllable of the stem is often quite reduced and very occasionally some assimilation between it and the initial vowel of the suffix may take place.' (Primary stress is stated over the word; only the secondary-stress rule refers to suffix/stem morphology. Since the language is 'entirely suffixing', word-initial = root-initial.)
morph.elicq: §2.1 p.5: '... except that final syllables are unstressed in connected speech. ... Many stems heard in citation form have pronounced stress on the final syllable as well as strong final aspiration (described by the informant as final \'h\'). These features are absent in connected speech, except at the end of an intonation pattern.' Data basis, §1.1 p.3-4: 'The Waŋkumara (Gaḷali) data presented in this paper are from fieldnotes and tapes recorded by S.A. Wurm in Canberra, April 1963 ... The data include 517 \'sentences\' and 342 vocabulary items ... The analysis presented is based purely on the text material and tapes.'…
morph.stmt: §1.2 p.4: 'Waŋkumara (Gaḷali) is entirely suffixing and morphologically fairly simple.' Verb: 'The minimal form of the verb is root plus inflection... There are a number of derivational stem-forming suffixes which intervene between root and inflection' (§3.3.1 p.33); nouns take post-posed case clitics (§3.2.3). In the 77-token text sample: 0 prefix morphs, 52 suffix/enclitic morphs (0 prefix syllables, 160 root syllables, 84 suffix syllables).

390.outw: rule hedged ('normally') with stated exceptions: emphasis shifts the stress (ŋíŋa 'him' vs ŋiŋá 'him EMPH'), final syllables are unstressed in connected speech, and the first syllable of a two-syllable suffix takes secondary stress (out: hedged-with-stated-exceptions, not domain-lumped)

391.dq: Accent, exclusively that of stress, is very strong and associated with a definite syllable in each word. In disyllabic words it is always on the first syllable and in polysyllabic words it is practically always on the antepenult. It can be stated, as a general rule, that the vowel accented is the stem vowel and that it rarely shifts no matter how many suffixes are added.
391.srule: Every root and compound member carries stress: between two junctures one stress is primary and the other roots/compound parts bear secondary stress, which in more than ninety percent of occurrences falls on alternate syllables counting from the primary-stressed syllable (Sawyer 1991:24; secondary written only where unpredictable). Radin 1929 records secondary accent only on the -e- preceding the future suffix (section 9, p.16; sometimes it takes the main accent) and on the final vowel of vowel-final singular imperatives (section 70, p.104).

morph.elicq: "Here we reproduce Sawyer's (1965:vii) sounds of Wappo. Since Sawyer's phonemic analysis was based on Laura's speech, we have taken it as the basis for the transcription we will use in this book. ... Sawyer's lexical entries are marked for stress, which we do not mark." (ch.1, p.1) — i.e. the stress generalization rests on the stress-marked headwords of Sawyer's (1965) English-Wappo vocabulary; the grammar itself states no procedure for checking stress (its own morphosyntactic data are 'sentences elicited by suggesting pragmatic contexts', Preface p.xiv).
morph.stmt: Wappo is predominantly suffixing: "Wappo is a rich case language. The morphologically unmarked case is the accusative; the other cases are marked by suffixes" (p.10), and the verb, "relatively rich in inflectional and derivational verbal morphology" (p.32), carries all tense/aspect, negation, imperative, infinitive, passive, purposive and suffixal-causative marking as suffixes (Table 4-7, p.67), while prefixes are limited to a closed set of directional prefixes (ma-, te-, mu-, tu-, ho-, meh-, č'a-, č'ah-, pah-, pi-; §4.4), the unspecified-object prefix o-, iterative pa-, the 'indefinite' i- and the causative oh-; verbs do not index subject or object person.

Romero-Figueroa 1997 states only the general data base (p.2 §3): "Insofar as possible, all data in the research are from elicited material, though extended texts are used to fill in certain gaps and to illustrate simple, completely straight-forward forms ... A corpus recorded on thirty six 90-minute tapes was collected", and (§4) "On no occasion was the data elicited by using interview schedules or written instruments of any sort"; the stress statement itself (p.112) cites "(Romero Figueroa, 1986b)" and is illustrated with an isolated inflected paradigm (309). morph.stmt: Warao is "predominantly suffixing, with few prefixes. Direct object cross-referencing markers are prefixed to the verb, while subject cross-referencing markers, plus tense-aspect, modality and directional morphemes, are suffixes... Possessive prefixes on nouns and object cross-referencing prefixes on verbs are almost identical... Causative is marked with a prefix (e-)" (Aikhenvald & Dixon 1999:378-9, summarising Romero-Figueroa 1997); the verb shows "chain-suffixing of person, aspect, mood and tense markers" (RF 1997:111, tue-a-e-ine 'burp-PUNC-PAST-1sg.S') and "imperative suffixes always attach last" (Robertson & Rybka 2020:80). 394.prule: Primary stress falls on the initial syllable of the word, the word including any enclitics and a cliticised auxiliary; in connected speech a non-initial word in the intonation phrase may carry no distinct primary stress (Nash 1980:100; Berry 1998:26, 109).
394.srule: Secondary stress is obligatory but morphologically placed: on the first syllable of every polysyllabic morpheme and on the first of a string of monosyllabic suffixes or clitics (a lone monosyllabic suffix before a polysyllabic morpheme is unstressed); never on a morpheme's second syllable or the word-final syllable; inside a long monomorphemic stretch it falls on odd-numbered syllables (mánangkàrra); monosyllabic preverbs and verb roots and the suffixes /nja/ /nji/ /ka/ attract it, and long vowels are always stressed (Nash 1980:100-101; Berry 1998:26-34, 85). Not computable from word length.
394.quote: In monomorphemic words, stress falls on the first syllable and on every following odd-numbered syllable. Main stress is on the first syllable. (1) a. mánangkàrra 'spinifex plain' [DGN:102] b. kúruwàrri 'variegated' [GB] c. wápurnùngku 'ghost gum' [GB] d. kárlarnjìrri 'lizard' [GB] e. wíjipìrtirli 'hospital' (loan) [GB] Stress on word-final syllables is not permitted. This means that in trisyllabic words there is only one stress. (2) a. wúrlampi 'stone knife' [GB] b. wátiya 'tree' [DGN:102] c. yújuku 'humpy' [GB] d. ngípiri 'egg' [GB]

evidence_works.detail: One Warlpiri speaker's 1960s narratives show the initial syllable with a higher f0 peak, a 4 dB intensity rise (the only language where intensity may be a real cue), modest vowel lengthening, stop-onset and glide post-tonic lengthening, and a tiny vowel-space effect. tn.quote: Both Dyirbal and Warlpiri employ an increase in pitch to indicate accentuation. In both languages a pitch accent occurs on the first syllable of an accented word. … 2.2.2. Warlpiri. Intonation in Warlpiri is phrasal rather than focal. Each syntactic phrase has an accent on the first word unless, under pragmatic constraints, the phrase is deaccented (i.e., dephrased) and is included in the domain of the accent of the previous phrase [5].

tn.note: No lexical tone described: pitch is intonational, a high pitch accent on the first (stressed) syllable of the first word of each phrase; two phonetic shapes of the high accent (rising, high-onset).

(sec. 3.3.1.2 p. 27) give secondary stress for non-future verbs of three or more syllables only: primary and secondary 'hard to distinguish', but 'there is always a stress (either primary or secondary) on the final syllable'; 3-syllable verbs first and last (/'nama'man/ 'they went'), 4-syllable verbs predominantly second and final (/ge'rago'so/), 5+ syllables 'final syllable stress with stress on preceding alternate syllables is the preferred rhythm', modulated by infixes that keep their own stress (/'nama-gi'lingi-'san/) and by stem length. morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was observed. The only relevant sentences: 'Waskia is a syllable-counting language with weak, non-contrastive stress, the rules governing which need further investigation' (p.2) and, on the data generally, 'John Natu Paol ... during the 1975-76 vacation collected data in Waskia, his native language, at his home village of Tokain ... morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing/encliticising in the verb and clause: 'Capell (1969) placed it in his typological category B iv(a) of languages which prefix the pronoun object to the verbal complex, but as this study will indicate, it properly belongs to his category B iv(d), in which subject, object and tense markers are all suffixal' (p.1); the verb word is 'verb root (plural object marker) subject-tense-mood suffix' (§2.22.1 p.42), followed by enclitic connectives; the only pre-root bound material is the elided possessor pronoun on inalienable nouns (a-tago 'my stomach') and a fossil numeral prefix i-.

396.srule: One secondary stress on the penultimate syllable of every word of three or more syllables: syllable 2 in trisyllables (adjacent to the primary), syllable 3 in quadrisyllables, the penult in longer words. Impressionistic statement; no stress-marked examples in the chapter.

morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing: §1.1 p.197 'Watjarri... is a suffixing type language similar to the Western Desert language'; §3.1[v] p.211 'verb inflection is by suffixation. No prefixes or proclitics are described anywhere in the grammar; in the 77 sampled tokens prefix count is 0 throughout.

The only morphological conditioning concerns phonological wordhood, not the root: §39 iii 'Most monosyllables are stressed, but many frequently-recurring monosyllables bear no stress, but are pronounced in conjunction with another word. These are proclitics, which precede the accented word, and enclitics, which follow it. The Welsh proclitics are the article y, yr, the prefixed pronouns fy, dy…
morph.elicq: No elicitation procedure is stated; the description rests on the author's knowledge of spoken Welsh and on metrical (cynghanedd) evidence for earlier periods: §40 ii 'The position of the accent was certainly the same in the Late Ml. period. This is proved by the fact that in the 14th cent. the cynghanedd was fully developed in its modern form in which the penultimate accent plays an important part'; §42 'The correct form médd-dod is still the form used in natural speech'; §44 ii 'In words of four or more syllables, when pronounced deliberately, the first syllable has a secondary accent, as bèndigédig'.

397.sec_rule: In words of four or more syllables, secondary stress ('rhythmic prominence') falls on every even-numbered syllable counting leftward from the penultimate primary stress (Bell et al. 2023: 506, with own transcriptions in Table 3: ysgrifennydd S-w-P-w, ysgrifenyddes w-S-w-P-w, ysgrifenyddesau S-w-S-w-P-w; after Ball & Williams 2001 ch. 12). The earlier description, Morris-Jones 1913 section 44 ii p. 54, places a single secondary accent on the first syllable of words of four or more syllables in deliberate speech (bendigedig, bendigedigion), none in regular trisyllables.
397.sec_quote: ii. In words of four or more syllables, when pronounced deliberately, the first syllable has a secondary accent, as bèn|di|gé|dig 'blessed', pl. bèn|di|ge|díg|ion. This also applies to trisyllables with the accent on the ultima, as cỳf|iaw|nhád 'justification'. 398.prule: Primary (principal) stress accent on the first syllable of every word, at all lengths, regardless of syllable shape or vowel length (length is conditioned by the accent); the enclitic particles -gad(a) and -min carry no accent of their own and lean on the preceding word; compounds keep the main accent on the first member.
398.srule: Words of 3-4 syllables: secondary accent on the 3rd syllable, except that (a) a short final open vowel takes none, (b, c) a 2nd syllable with e before nj, ng or dj attracts the secondary to the 2nd (a subsidiary secondary may then fall on the 4th), (d) the connecting vowel a before -ngur/-ngal/-wal never bears it; words of 5+ syllables: the 4th syllable usually has a very strong secondary and the 6th a subsidiary secondary. Vocatives take a strong secondary on the final syllable (p.29); second members of compounds bear only secondary stress (p.14). Conditioned, so not coded in the grid.

morph.stmt: Wembawemba is exclusively suffixing (plus two enclitics and some reduplication); Hercus never mentions a prefix: 'The cases of nouns in Wembawemba are generally formed by the addition of certain suffixes or relationship-markers' (p.27); 'A uniform system of endings expresses the number and person of the subject throughout the tense system' (p.41); 'The tense marker for the present tense is -a, for the past -in, and for the future -inj' (p.41); possessive suffixes follow case suffixes and the genitive follows the possessive (pp.33-34); 'The particles -gad and -min are unaccented and enclitic to other words, generally to the head-word of a clause' (p.60).

The first-hand accent material (pp.74-75, sec. 3.1.7) concerns Mathi-Mathi: initial primary stress before single velars/labials and most clusters, second-syllable primary stress after coronal single onsets, hiatus, -nd-, -lp-, hesitation with -rrk-, -mb-, -lk-, and the added heavy-second-syllable condition ('If the second syllable was heavy, i.e. if it was a closed syllable or contained a diphthong it also tended to attract the stress accent. In the case of closed syllables this was not an absolute rule as we have tìpárrkima "to glue together" but ngákundàl "mountain duck" is an exception', p.75), summarised p.75 as: primary stress on the 2nd syllable 'if the second syllable contains a diphthong or is a closed syllable' or 'if the second syllable begins with a coronal consonant'.

399.dq: 3.5. Stress. Stress in Weri is non-phonemic, occurring on the final syllable of a word. Each preceding alternate syllable carries a secondary stress. Often in four and five syllable words the stress on the antepenultimate syllable is equal to or heavier than that on the ultimate.

399.srule: Secondary stress on each alternate syllable preceding the final (primary) stress; in four- and five-syllable words the antepenultimate stress is often equal to or heavier than the final one (Boxwell & Boxwell 1966:88).
399.quote: 3.5. Stress. Stress in Weri is non-phonemic, occurring on the final syllable of a word. Each preceding alternate syllable carries a secondary stress. Often in four and five syllable words the stress on the antepenultimate syllable is equal to or heavier than that on the ultimate.
399.idn: Weri, Sim dialect (village of Sim, upper Waria valley, Morobe District); Glottolog dialect Sim simm1238 under weri1253 (a named variety of the language); data: 'The corpus of data, including a dictionary of about 1000 words, was gathered in the village of Sim over a period of 7½ months from January 1962 to September…
399.exq_: Stress in Weri is non-phonemic, occurring on the final syllable of a word. Each preceding alternate syllable carries a secondary stress. Often in four and five syllable words the stress on the antepenultimate syllable is equal to or heavier than that on the ultimate.
399.tone: Tone language: two phonemic ('emic') tones, high (acute accent) and low (unmarked), with minimal pairs (e.g. /wáput/ 'needles' vs /watút/ 'horns'); pitch range between high and low 'quite narrow'; 'Tone perturbation has not been observed'; the syllable is 'defined as a unit of tone placement'. Stress is described separately as non-phonemic and final (Boxwell & Boxwell 1966 sec. 3.4-3.5, pp. 87-88; Boxwell 1992 OPD: 'Weri has two phonemic tones, high and low').

Often in four and five syllable words the stress on the antepenultimate syllable is equal to or heavier than that on the ultimate.' The domain is the word; no reference to root, stem or affixes (illustrative words include inflected forms, e.g. /saut/ 'I went', /ökunetepau/ 'times').
morph.elicq: No explicit methodological statement. The description rests on the authors' field corpus — 'The corpus of data, including a dictionary of about 1000 words, was gathered in the village of Sim over a period of 7½ months from January 1962 to September 1963' (Boxwell & Boxwell 1966 sec. 0) — and the stress section is illustrated only with single words in citation-form phonetic transcription: /ŋintip/ [ŋin'tip] 'bee', /uluamit/ [ulua'mit] 'mist', /ökunetepau/ [ökunete'pau] 'times' (sec. 3.5). No frame sentences, texts or measurements are mentioned.
morph.stmt: Weri is predominantly suffixing — nouns take classifier-number, case, possessive, focus and 'only' suffixes and 'Final verbs carry person-number-tense affixation' as suffixes while 'medial verbs have a minimum of affixation with the presence or absence of a morpheme signalling different subject [-ën]' (Boxwell 1980 n.5) — but the verb has a small prefix field: the present/actual tense marker ya-/ye-, the object 'bound pronouns' which 'are a small set of verb prefixes' ne-/mo-/ni- (Boxwell 1990:340), and the negative na- of the circumfix na-…-n ('both a negative prefix and suffix', Boxwell 1969 sec. 2.5).

tn.quote: 3.4. Tone. Tone is a feature of many New Guinea languages especially in the main highland area. Weri, a member of the Kunimaipa-Fuyege-Tauade-Weri-Biangai family, has two emic tones, high tone indicated by an acute accent over the vowel, and low tone which is left unmarked. Unlike most tone languages, the pitch range between high and low tone is quite narrow. Tone perturbation has not been observed. ... 3.5. Stress. Stress in Weri is non-phonemic, occurring on the final syllable of a word. Each preceding alternate syllable carries a secondary stress.

The only secondary-stress statement is Vinas Urquiza 1974:32 (Mision Chaquena), quoted by StressTyp2 entry and Avram 2008:78: in suffixed words, where primary stress has moved to the final syllable, a secondary stress stays on the root syllable that carried primary stress in the unsuffixed base ('El acento secundario ocupa la posicion primitiva del acento primario, antes de su desplazamiento'); Tovar 1981:172 rejects this two-stress analysis (stress is phrasal). 402.prule: Primary (main) stress on the first syllable of the word, a heavy stress accent accompanied by high pitch (Hercus 1999:35).
402.srule: Secondary stress on the third syllable of words of more than three syllables (Hercus 1999:35); disyllabic case markers -ngorni/-birna bear at least a secondary stress, and in the optional -(g)ardu pattern the initial syllable keeps a secondary accent when the main stress moves to the long aa.
402.quote: The regular accent in Wirangu is on the first syllable of a word, as is the case in all the surrounding languages. It is a fairly heavy stress accent (here marked by ‘ preceding the stressed syllable). The accent is accompanied by a high pitch intonation. There is a secondary stress on the third syllable of words of more than three syllables (this is here marked by “ preceding the syllable that bears the secondary accent). There are however a few situations in which this can vary. In emphatic vocatives and imperatives the accent can shift to the final syllable, which can then show vowel disto…
402.idn: Wirangu (two historical dialects noted: Gawler Ranges/Venus Bay vs. areas further west; the Gawler Ranges dialect now lost); data: fieldwork visits to Ceduna and Bookabie (west coast of South Australia) from September 1993 with Gladys Miller, Doreen Miller and others; also J.T. Platt's tapes of thirty years earlier…
402.exq_: In emphatic vocatives and imperatives the accent can shift to the final syllable ... In words formed with the addition of the suffix -gardu, -garda ... the main stress optionally falls onto the long a that is created by elision of the initial g of that suffix, if the stem ends in -a

morph.rootq: Main rule is stated over the WORD, not the root: 'The regular accent in Wirangu is on the first syllable of a word, as is the case in all the surrounding languages. It is a fairly heavy stress accent ... There is a secondary stress on the third syllable of words of more than three syllables' (§2.2.2(a) p.35). But the description also makes suffix-specific stress statements: 'In words formed with the addition of the suffix -gardu, -garda ... the main stress optionally falls onto the long a that is created by elision of the initial g of that suffix, if the stem ends in -a: marna ['marna] big, marnaardu ["ma'rnaardu] very big ... The initial syllable in these words has a secondary accent.…
morph.elicq: The accent section (§2.2.2, pp.35-36) gives no statement of how stress was observed; examples are isolated words and emphatic vocatives/imperatives (['wiya] mother vs ["wi'yai] eh, mother!). On the data in general: 'We then did some systematic language elicitation and also listened to and worked from the tapes made by the late John Platt thirty years earlier' (Preface p.xv); 'Inevitably there are some gaps, and there is no available continuous text' (Ch.7 Conclusion p.151). No instrumental measurement is mentioned.
morph.stmt: Wirangu is exclusively suffixing in Hercus's description: nominal case markers are suffixes 'simply added to the stem, however many syllables it has' (§3.1.6 p.47), the verb is 'STEM ± ASPECTUAL AFFIX ± ASPECTUAL AFFIX ± VOICE MARKER + ASSOCIATED MOTION COMPLEX + TENSE ± CLITIC' with every element following the (C)V(C)C root and its stem vowel (§5.1.2 pp.94-96), and 'Clitics are postinflectional suffixes' (§6.3 p.147); no prefix or proclitic is described (only the rare particle ba 'and' 'may be considered proclitic', §2.2.2(b) p.36).

evidence_works.detail: Catalog rule (initial primary, secondary on syllable 3 in words of 4+ syllables; sec_status 'stated: rule given') matches the text exactly. Exceptions stated on pp. 35-36 not in the entry: (1) emphatic vocatives and imperatives shift the accent to the final syllable with vowel distortion ['wiya] 'mother' vs ["wi'yai] 'eh, mother!'; (2) with suffix -gardu/-garda after an a-final stem, the main stress optionally falls on the long aa created by g-elision, the initial syllable then carrying secondary accent (marnaardu ["ma'rnaardu] 'very big'), or optionally stays initial with high pitch; (3) p. 4

403.exq_: The intonational pivot occurs on the last inherent high or unmarked syllable of the intonational phrase. The pivot is marked by high tone.
403.tone: Two phonemic tones (high, low), with syllables lexically marked for three tone-feature types: inherent high (acute accent), inherent low (grave accent; always low, and may force a high tone onto a preceding syllable within the intonational pivot), and unmarked (surface high or low predictable from position relative to the intonational pivot and to inherent low-tone syllables). The only positional prominence is the phrase-level intonational pivot, a high tone on the last inherent-high or unmarked syllable of the intonational phrase (Payne 1985:30-31).

The intonational pivot occurs on the last inherent high or unmarked syllable of the intonational phrase. The pivot is marked by high tone. morph.stmt: 'Contrary to VIN [the verb-initial norm], affixation in Yagua is almost exclusively suffixing' (sect. 5.5, p. 238; verb template (380) ROOT-DERIVATIONAL-LOCATION-MOVEMENT/COMPLETIVE/ITERATION-IMPERFECTIVITY-MODAL-TENSE); the only pre-root bound material is the Set I person proclitics ('Set I clitics are prefixal', p. 41), which mark subjects on verbs/auxiliaries, possessors on nouns and objects of postpositions, so a typical word is PROCLITIC=root-suffix-suffix(-enclitic).

tn.quote: There are two phonemic tones, but syllables are lexically marked for three types of tone features. Syllables which have an inherent high tone are marked with the accute accent. These are syllables which must have a surface high tone, or sometimes a low-high or high-low glide on certain long vowels. ... Syllables with inherent low tone are marked with the grave accent. These are syllables which must always have a low tone ... Syllables which do not have inherent tone assignment are not marked, even when they receive (predictable) surface high tone in certain contexts.
tn.cite: Payne, Doris L. 1985. Aspects of the Grammar of Yagua: A Typological Perspective. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles.
tn.note: Two level tones (high, low); syllables inherent-high, inherent-low or unmarked, the unmarked taking surface tone from the phrasal intonational pivot. Long-vowel glides are realizations. No stress rule

403.cfw: Payne 1985 and Powlison 1995, the only two first-hand descriptions, agree that Yagua has two lexical tones and no word-stress rule, its only final-like prominence being a phrase-level intonational pivot, so the fixed-final-stress code in StressTyp2 (Goedemans, Heinz & van der Hulst 2015) and Gordon 2002 reads as a database reclassifying of that pivot rather than an independent observation.
